body.en: AP Precalculus is a College Board course that deepens understanding of functions as dynamic objects whose properties model the real world. Unlike a traditional precalculus course, AP Precalculus emphasises rates of change, transformations, and function behaviour — the conceptual language of calculus.

value.en: Polynomial and rational functions — change, zeros, end behaviour, asymptotes.
Exponential and logarithmic functions — multiplicative change, inverses, models.
Trigonometric and polar functions — periodic change, sinusoidal models, polar graphs.
Functions involving parameters — parametric motion, vectors, matrix transformations.

body.en: Exam format: Section I — 40 MCQ (Part A: 28 Qs in 80 min, no calculator; Part B: 12 Qs in 50 min, graphing calculator). Section II — 4 FRQ in 60 min (graphing calculator permitted throughout).

• Section I Part A (No Calculator — 28 Qs / 80 min): About 2.8 minutes per question. Focus on exact algebraic manipulation, unit circle values, factor theorem, and sign charts.
  • Section I Part B (Graphing Calculator — 12 Qs / 50 min): Over 4 minutes per question. Problems require numerical solving, graphing intersections, and regression curve fitting.
  • Section II (4 FRQs / 60 min): Allot 15 minutes per free-response question. All 4 FRQs permit a graphing calculator. Round non-exact numerical answers to 3 decimal places unless specified otherwise.

label.en: ▲ The 4 Core FRQ Commandments of AP Precalculus

body.en:
• 1. Always Use Function Notation & Units: When modeling real-world quantities, define variables with units (e.g., 'let \(t\) be time in hours since midnight'). Include units in your final answers.
  • 2. Justify Using Rates of Change (AROC): When asked whether a model is appropriate, explain using rates of change: linear functions have constant first differences, quadratic functions have constant second differences, and exponential functions have constant proportional growth ratios.
  • 3. Show Setup Before Calculator Results: Even with a graphing calculator, you must show the mathematical equation or definite expression before writing the computed number (e.g. write '\(f(t) = 150 \Rightarrow 400(0.85)^t = 150\)' before stating \(t \approx 6.027\)).
  • 4. Use 3-Decimal Precision: College Board standard is 3 decimal places (truncated or rounded). Store unrounded intermediate values in your calculator variables to prevent intermediate rounding errors.

question.en: A student spends 80 minutes on Section I Part A (28 multiple-choice questions) and 50 minutes on Section I Part B (12 multiple-choice questions). Calculate the average time available per question in Part A and Part B to the nearest tenth of a minute.

solution.en: Part A: \(\frac{80\text{ min}}{28\text{ questions}} \approx 2.86 \approx 2.9\text{ minutes/question}\). Part B: \(\frac{50\text{ min}}{12\text{ questions}} \approx 4.17 \approx 4.2\text{ minutes/question}\).
